questions.q: A survey asks 100 people whether they own a cat, a dog, both, or neither. 60 say they own a cat, 50 say they own a dog, and 15 say they own neither. How many own both a cat and a dog?

Program A and Program B both run SAT prep courses. On an easy practice test, Program A's students pass at 90% (45 of 50) while Program B's pass at 88% (440 of 500). On a hard practice test, Program A passes 20% (10 of 50) while Program B passes 15% (3 of 20). Program A has a higher pass rate on both tests. Yet combining both tests, Program B has more total passes relative to total students. How is this possible?
choices: This is a contradiction and the data must be wrong
Program B is actually better on every individual test; the breakdown must be mistaken
Pure random chance explains the reversal regardless of the group sizes
Program B tested overwhelmingly more students on the easy test, which pulls its combined rate up — a Simpson's paradox effect from unequal group sizes

questions.q: Steve is quiet, keeps meticulously organized records, and has little interest in people — traits many associate with librarians. Based purely on the rules of probability (not on how 'typical' each sounds), which must be true, given that farmers vastly outnumber librarians in the general population?
choices: There is not enough information to compare them
P(Steve is a farmer AND a librarian) ≥ P(Steve is a farmer)
Both probabilities must be exactly equal
P(Steve is a farmer) ≥ P(Steve is a farmer AND a librarian)

questions.q: A plane crashes exactly on the border between two countries. Where are the survivors buried?
choices: Whichever country they were citizens of

questions.q: A classic puzzle cuts an 8×8 square (area 64) into 4 pieces and rearranges them into a 5×13 rectangle (area 65) — using the exact same four pieces. Since area cannot actually appear from nowhere, what is really going on?
choices: The original square doesn't actually measure exactly 8×8; rounding in the drawing causes the discrepancy.
One of the four pieces is quietly resized between the two arrangements.
Area is not conserved when flat shapes are cut and rigidly rearranged.
The four pieces don't perfectly form a true rectangle — a thin sliver-shaped gap along the diagonal, invisible at normal drawing scale, accounts for the 'missing' unit of area.

questions.q: In a single round of the Prisoner's Dilemma, two purely rational, self-interested players cannot communicate or retaliate later. Mutual cooperation would leave both better off than mutual defection. What does classical game theory say two such rational players will actually do?
choices: Both will defect — defection dominates cooperation for each player individually, even though it leaves them both worse off
They split — one cooperates while the other defects
Both will cooperate, since cooperation is the jointly optimal choice
Each randomizes 50/50 between cooperating and defecting
